opus-5.5.text:
So the way I think about model diffing is that it should help you understand what actually changed when you go from one version of a model to another. You have a base model, you fine-tune it, you do some RL, you apply some safety training. Today we mostly evaluate that change from the outside. We run benchmarks, we look at outputs, and we say, okay, it scores better on this and worse on that. But that tells you very little about what happened internally.

What model diffing should let you do is look at the two models and say, here are the specific features, circuits, or representations that shifted. Maybe the fine-tune taught the model a new concept. Maybe it just reweighted something that was already there. Or maybe it suppressed a behavior without actually removing the underlying capability, which matters a lot from a safety perspective. If you do refusal training and the model has learned to hide a capability rather than lose it, you want to know that.

The other big thing is unintended side effects. When you train for one objective, you often get changes you didn't ask for, like sycophancy creeping in, or the model picking up some weird association from the training data. Those can be really hard to catch with evals, because you have to know what to look for in advance. Diffing flips that around. Instead of guessing what might have gone wrong and writing a test for it, you look directly at what changed and ask whether you expected it.

So ultimately I'd like it to be something like a code review for model weights. When engineers change software, you look at the diff and reason about it line by line. We don't have that for neural networks yet, and I think it's one of the most practical places interpretability can make a difference right now. You don't need to understand the entire model from scratch. You just need to understand the delta, which is a much more tractable problem.

r001.rationale: The response says diffing can reveal changes introduced between model versions, including a new concept taught by fine-tuning and unexpected associations from training data—things that may not have been present in the earlier model.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: Thanks for having me. So the way I think about model diffing is that most of the interesting questions people actually have about a model aren't about the model in isolation, they're about a change. You took a base model and you fine-tuned it, or you did RLHF on it, or you trained on some new data mixture, and the question is: what did that do? Not "what is this model" but "what is different about this model."

And right now the way people answer that is almost entirely behavioral. You run evals before and after, you look at the deltas, maybe you red-team it. That tells you what changed on the distribution you thought to test. It tells you nothing about what changed on the distribution you didn't think to test, which is usually where the problems are.

So what I want diffing to give you is a mechanistic account of the change. Concretely, I want to be able to say: fine-tuning introduced these new features, or it amplified these existing ones, or it rewired how this circuit reads from that one. Ideally you get a relatively small, human-readable set of differences, because the hypothesis is that most fine-tunes are actually pretty low-rank in some meaningful sense. The model didn't become a different model. It learned a handful of new things and maybe suppressed a handful of old ones.

If you can get that, a few things become possible. One is auditing. If someone hands you a fine-tune and says it's a customer service model, you can look at the diff and ask whether anything in there looks unrelated to customer service. A backdoor, a sleeper behavior, some weird preference that got picked up from the data. That's a much more tractable problem than auditing the whole model from scratch, because you're looking at the change rather than the whole thing.

The second is understanding training itself. We mostly treat training as a black box that we tune hyperparameters on. If you could watch the diffs accumulate over the course of training and see which features form when, that starts to look like an actual science of how models learn rather than alchemy.

And the third, which I think is underappreciated, is that diffing gives you a kind of ground truth that pure interpretability often lacks. When you interpret a single model you're always a little worried that you're telling yourself a story. With diffing you have an intervention, you know what you did, and your interpretation of the diff has to be consistent with that. It's a much more constrained problem, and I think that constraint is what makes it tractable.

r001.rationale: The candidate says diffing should identify features introduced by fine-tuning and gives unexpected examples such as a backdoor, sleeper behavior, or an unrelated preference—changes absent from the earlier model.

astra-6.text:
I think model diffing should let you understand what changed between two versions of a neural network in a mechanistic way. If you take a model and fine-tune it, you can measure how its behavior changes, but that doesn’t necessarily tell you what it learned. Did it acquire a new capability? Did it learn to use a capability it already had? Or did it just learn when to give a particular kind of answer?

What I’d really want is to connect those behavioral differences to changes inside the model—to identify the representations or circuits that changed, and then test whether those changes actually cause the behavior we’re seeing. So you’re moving from ‘these models give different answers’ to an explanation of why they give different answers.

r001.rationale: The response says model diffing should identify mechanistic changes between versions, but it does not state that it should reveal surprising things in the network that were absent at an earlier checkpoint.

sol-6.1.text: I think model diffing should help us understand what changed between two models at the level of the computation they’re doing. If you fine-tune a model and it starts behaving differently, can we identify which internal mechanisms changed and explain how those changes produce the new behavior? Ideally, that explanation would let us make predictions and test them—for example, by intervening on the relevant parts of the network and seeing whether the behavior changes in the way we expect.

r001.rationale: The response says model diffing should identify changed mechanisms and explain new behavior, but it does not state that it should reveal surprising things present in the network that were absent at an earlier checkpoint.
